q1: SELECT b.name AS bar, COUNT(DISTINCT f.drinker) AS num_drinker, AVG(s.price) AS avg_price, (SELECT f1.drinker FROM frequents AS f1 WHERE f1.bar = b.name ORDER BY f1.times_a_week DESC, f1.drinker ASC LIMIT 1) AS most_reg_drinker FROM bar AS b LEFT JOIN frequents AS f ON b.name = f.bar LEFT JOIN serves AS s ON b.name = s.bar GROUP BY b.name ORDER BY num_drinker DESC, b.name ASC
q2: SELECT b.name AS bar_name, COALESCE(total_num_drinker, 0) AS total_num_drinker, COALESCE(avg_price, NULL) AS avg_price, COALESCE(most_reg_drinker, NULL) AS most_reg_drinker FROM bar AS b LEFT JOIN (SELECT f.bar, COUNT(DISTINCT f.drinker) AS total_num_drinker FROM frequents AS f GROUP BY f.bar) AS drinkers_count ON b.name = drinkers_count.bar LEFT JOIN (SELECT s.bar, AVG(s.price) AS avg_price FROM serves AS s GROUP BY s.bar) AS price_avg ON b.name = price_avg.bar LEFT JOIN (SELECT f.bar, f.drinker AS most_reg_drinker, MAX(f.times_a_week) AS times_a_week FROM frequents AS f GROUP BY f.bar, f.drinker ORDER BY f.bar, times_a_week DESC, f.drinker) AS most_frequent_drinker ON b.name = most_frequent_drinker.bar ORDER BY total_num_drinker DESC, bar_name

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because of the way they handle the subquery for the most regular drinker. Q1 orders the subquery results by times_a_week DESC and drinker ASC, while Q2 orders by times_a_week DESC and drinker. This difference can lead to different results when there are ties in times_a_week.
counterexample_dsp: The test data should have two bars, 'B1' and 'B2', each with two regular drinkers, 'D1' and 'D2', who have the same number of visits (times_a_week) but 'D1' has a lexicographically smaller name than 'D2'.
